say.en: India has tried growth, special employment and self-employment schemes, and direct support for basic needs. Which approach works, and why do all three matter? In this lesson: Describe the three-pronged approach to poverty removal.
Name major schemes and what they do.
Evaluate the success and limits of anti-poverty programmes.

body.en: The first prong is growth: faster growth was expected to raise incomes and spread benefits to the poor (the trickle-down idea), but growth alone did not reach everyone. The second is specific programmes to create assets and work for the poor: wage employment and self-employment schemes. The third is meeting minimum basic needs directly: subsidised food through the public distribution system, health, housing, drinking water, sanitation and pensions.

points.en: Minimum basic needs and social security

body.en: The Mahatma Gandhi National Rural Employment Guarantee Act (2005) guarantees up to 100 days of paid work a year to every rural household that asks for it. The National Rural Livelihoods Mission supports self-help groups and self-employment. Housing *schemes*, the public distribution system, pensions for the old and widows, and direct benefit transfers into bank accounts provide support. Poverty has fallen, but problems remain: leakages, poor targeting, little asset creation and weak participation by the poor in designing schemes.

points.en: MGNREGA: up to 100 days of wage work for rural households
Self-help groups and self-employment through NRLM
PDS, housing, pensions and direct benefit transfers
Limits: leakage, targeting errors, weak delivery

problem.en: A district's poverty gap is ₹100 crore. Plan A spends ₹120 crore with 25% leakage and 60% targeting. Plan B spends ₹100 crore with 10% leakage and 80% targeting. Which closes more of the gap?

steps.en: Plan A: 120 × 0.75 × 0.60 = ₹54 crore reaches the poor.
Plan B: 100 × 0.90 × 0.80 = ₹72 crore reaches the poor.
Plan B closes 72% of the gap against 54% for Plan A, with less money.

answer.en: Plan B: better delivery beats a bigger budget here.

say.en: Let us work this out step by step. A district's poverty gap is 100 rupees crore. Plan A spends 120 rupees crore with 25 percent leakage and 60 percent targeting. Plan B spends 100 rupees crore with 10 percent leakage and 80 percent targeting. Which closes more of the gap?
Plan A: 120 times 0.75 times 0.60 equals 54 rupees crore reaches the poor.
Plan B: 100 times 0.90 times 0.80 equals 72 rupees crore reaches the poor.
Plan B closes 72 percent of the gap against 54 percent for Plan A, with less money.
So the answer is Plan B: better delivery beats a bigger budget here.
